sources.title: Michael Brass, The Emergence of Mobile Pastoral Elites during the Middle to Late Holocene in the Sahara (2019)
sources.note: Full author manuscript directly read. Table 3 and Wadi Tanezzuft discussion, especially printed manuscript pp. 13 to 20. Regional period boundaries are approximate; pastoral societies vary through space and time. Research interpretations of elite hierarchy are not treated as directly observable offices or named dynasties.

sources.title: Mauro Cremaschi and Andrea Zerboni, Early to Middle Holocene landscape exploitation in a drying environment (2009)
sources.note: Original geoarchaeological research. Indexed full section 7 checked, including buried soils, settlements, oasis boundaries and later contraction. Same work as ScienceDirect S1631071309001023 and DOI 10.1016/j.crte.2009.05.001; check duplicate-work reuse. Publication distinguishes soil disturbance from proof of ploughing.

sources.title: di Lernia and colleagues, Land-use and cultivation in the etaghas of the Tadrart Acacus (2020)
sources.note: Full original research article directly read. Discussion separates Final Pastoral archaeological evidence from present Kel Tadrart cultivation. Do not transfer present planting recipes or ownership customs to prehistory. Ancient cultivation remains partly a hypothesis supported by tools, palaeosoils and site pattern.

sources.title: di Lernia and colleagues, Megalithic architecture and funerary practices in the late prehistory of Wadi Tanezzuft (2001)
sources.note: Original excavation report abstract fully indexed and checked through Cambridge author/volume listing. Direct article fetch failed. Site 96/129 excavated 1999 to 2000, end of Late Pastoral, approximately 3000 uncalibrated BP; do not directly convert this to an exact BCE date. Labour-related afflictions, multiple burials, burnt animal bones and ash directly stated.

sources.title: Paris, Person, Quéchon and Saliège, Les débuts de la métallurgie au Niger septentrional (1991)
sources.note: Original archaeological paper indexed full text checked, printed pp. 57 to 59. Iwelen copper use and possible working explicitly distinguished from smelting; no furnaces or slag found there. Afunfun TAG 9 stone-delimited features interpreted as tent or hut wall supports. Do not convert radiocarbon BP measurements to exact calendar dates.

sources.title: Marina Gallinaro, Saharan Rock Art: Local Dynamics and Wider Perspectives (2013)
sources.note: Full indexed research article checked, especially sections 2 and 4, printed pp. 360 to 361 and Figure 6. Direct page failed; indexed publisher PDF confirms text. Same work at MDPI PDF and ResearchGate 259327693. Horse/Bitriangular styles roughly fourth millennium to mid-third millennium BP; chronology approximate. Libyco-Berber earliest occurrence attributed broadly to Garamantian phase, not a securely dated message by an identified prehistoric nomad.

sources.title: Julie Dunne and colleagues, First dairying in green Saharan Africa in the fifth millennium BC (2012)
sources.note: Primary residue study and publisher editorial summary checked. Milk lipids in Takarkori pottery date to fifth millennium BCE, much earlier than imported map window. This is explicitly earlier background, not a claim of discovery around 2000 BCE.

proposedOverrides.name: Saharan pastoral communities
proposedOverrides.summary: Diverse Saharan herding communities, with local histories of water management, farming, craft and mobility.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Broad imported lifeway label, not a unitary ethnic or political identity. Distinct from saharan-nomadic-tribes (700 to 800 CE). Decoded outlier fragments extend to Somalia and the eastern Nile margins in some snapshots. Public geometry warning retained. Regional pastoral period boundaries approximate; Final Pastoral chronological limits follow Brass Table 3. Takarkori milk example explicitly fifth millennium BCE, before map; no exact dates invented for skeletons or Afunfun features. Writing discussion limits attribution, not the existence of Libyco-Berber writing.
